splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on when actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability under ERISA must be finalized. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans, as the timing directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, so long as they are applied to data as of that date.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be fixed by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year) to provide employers with predictability about potential withdrawal liability.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the period of court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled during the period a supervisee absconds, so courts retain authority to revoke supervised release even after the original term would have expired.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release terms when a supervisee absconds, and courts lack authority to extend the period of supervision beyond what Congress prescribed.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: A longstanding 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than Congress intended when bringing successive collateral attacks. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners are categorically barred from raising any claim they previously presented, in addition to Section 2255(h)'s separate requirements.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar on relitigating previously raised claims under § 2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar does not apply to federal prisoners filing § 2255 motions, so they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates can demonstrate sufficient injury-in-fact to challenge election rules before an election takes place. The resolution affects whether pre-election challenges to voting procedures are viable or must wait until after the election, when effective relief may be impossible.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to challenge election laws that allegedly dilute or undermine their electoral prospects, including laws governing ballot-counting deadlines.

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not have Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to ballot-counting rules because the alleged competitive injury is too speculative.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous Sentencing Guidelines provisions in criminal cases.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's anti-defendant interpretations of ambiguous Guidelines provisions or instead apply the rule of lenity in favor of defendants. This split has deepened after Loper Bright overruled Chevron deference.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions, preventing agencies from using delegated power to expand criminal liability.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary controls over the rule of lenity when interpreting ambiguous Guidelines provisions, even in criminal contexts.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether 'and' in the safety-valve provision means 'and' or 'or,' determining whether defendants must meet all three criminal-history criteria to be disqualified from safety-valve relief or whether possessing any single criterion suffices. This split leads to dramatically different sentences for identically situated defendants depending on geography.

positions.label: Conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that the word 'and' in § 3553(f)(1) is unambiguously conjunctive, so defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three listed criminal-history criteria.

positions.label: Disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that 'and' in § 3553(f)(1) operates disjunctively (or distributively), so possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which expands the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, is entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary adding conspiracy and other inchoate offenses to the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' is a valid authoritative interpretation deserving deference. This split affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy convictions can be sentenced as career offenders.

positions.label: Commentary is entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is the Sentencing Commission's authoritative interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and is entitled to controlling weight, so inchoate offenses like conspiracy qualify as controlled substance offenses.

positions.label: Commentary exceeds the guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses because § 4B1.2(b) does not mention conspiracy, and the commentary impermissibly expands the guideline's scope beyond its plain meaning.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute or contribute to 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether district courts may consider non-retroactive changes in law as a factor supporting compassionate release. Some circuits categorically bar such consideration, while others permit it as one factor among many. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) attempted to resolve this but has itself generated further disagreement about the Commission's authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may be considered
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law, alone or combined with other factors, may contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot be considered
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, whether offered alone or in combination with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state statute covers substances not listed on the federal controlled substances schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) requires the underlying substance to be federally controlled or whether any state-controlled substance suffices. This affects career offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: State schedules suffice
positions.summary: Holds that 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines includes offenses under state law regardless of whether the substance is also controlled under federal law, because the text refers to 'an offense under state law' without limiting it to federally scheduled substances.

positions.label: Must be federally controlled substance
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the underlying substance is also controlled under federal law, requiring a categorical match with federal schedules.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appellate deadline applies to appeals from orders denying Hyde Amendment motions for attorney's fees in criminal cases.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (triggering the 30-day civil deadline) or part of the criminal case itself (triggering the shorter 14-day criminal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion remains part of the criminal case, so the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging conditions of confinement or BOP decisions affecting the execution of their sentences must proceed via habeas corpus or may bring claims under Bivens or other civil rights statutes.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether challenges to conditions of confinement or BOP decisions that do not directly challenge the fact or duration of confinement must be brought as habeas petitions or can be pursued through civil rights actions. This affects federal prisoners' access to remedies for statutory rights under the First Step Act and other statutes.

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive remedy for execution-of-sentence claims
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to BOP decisions regarding the execution of a prisoner's sentence, including transfer to prerelease custody, must be brought through habeas corpus and cannot proceed as civil rights actions.

positions.label: Civil rights actions available for conditions claims
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may challenge conditions of confinement and certain BOP decisions through civil rights actions (§ 1983 or Bivens) rather than being limited to habeas corpus, at least where the claim does not directly challenge the fact or duration of confinement.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's assets belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. This split has significant practical consequences for debtors who convert in good faith but whose property has appreciated.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that under the broad scope of § 541(a), post-petition appreciation in property value and corresponding increases in equity belong to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that under § 348(f)(1)(A), post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtor upon good-faith conversion, consistent with the statute's structure, policies, and legislative history.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly impose punishment for the violation of supervised release conditions at revocation, or whether revocation sanctions must be limited to addressing the breach of the court's trust.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the permissible purposes of sentences imposed upon revocation of supervised release. Some circuits allow district courts to punish defendants for the underlying violation conduct, while others hold that revocation sanctions must be limited to sanctioning the breach of trust inherent in violating release conditions.

positions.label: Punishment for violation is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for their violation conduct when revoking supervised release, and that the Sentencing Guidelines permit consideration of the seriousness of the violation.

positions.label: Revocation limited to breach of trust
positions.summary: Holds that the purpose of revocation sentencing is to sanction the breach of trust inherent in violating supervised release conditions, not to punish the underlying violation conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination in the operation of hospitality or business establishments, specifically regarding the scope of 42 U.S.C. § 1981 and Title II of the Civil Rights Act in hotel and service settings.
splits.description: The Second Circuit's approach to discrimination claims in hospitality settings has generated sufficient disagreement to warrant Supreme Court review. The case will clarify standards for fair treatment, discrimination liability, and damages in hospitality, retail, and other service industries.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that discrimination claims in hospitality settings may proceed under broader standards, permitting recovery for dignitary harms and applying less demanding proof requirements for establishing discriminatory intent.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that discrimination claims in hospitality and service contexts require more rigorous proof of discriminatory intent and impose narrower standards for establishing liability and damages.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's labeling requirements preempt state tort claims alleging that a pesticide manufacturer should have included additional warnings on its product label that the EPA did not require. This affects the ability of plaintiffs to bring state-law claims against pesticide manufacturers nationwide.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts state failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims because allowing state courts to require different or additional label warnings would impose requirements 'in addition to or different from' those under FIFRA.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt state failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state failure-to-warn claims because such claims are based on duties that parallel federal requirements, and manufacturers can comply with both state and federal obligations.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: In re Roundup Products Liability Litigation

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption provision, which bars states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the motor carriers they select.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that the FAAAA preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers because such claims are 'related to' the broker's services within the meaning of the statute's broad preemption clause.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that common-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they do not relate to the broker's prices, routes, or services in the manner Congress intended to preempt.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts may consider claims that might also be raised in a habeas petition under § 2255 — such as legal errors at trial or sentencing — as extraordinary and compelling reasons supporting compassionate release. This affects prisoners who may lack access to traditional habeas remedies.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts have discretion to consider legal errors or unfairness in the defendant's underlying conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: May not consider — must use § 2255
positions.summary: Holds that compassionate release cannot be used as a vehicle to challenge the validity of a conviction or sentence, and such claims must be brought through the habeas process under § 2255.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Post-Bruen, circuits have split on whether the federal ban on firearm possession by unlawful drug users passes constitutional muster under the Second Amendment's historical-tradition test. Some circuits have upheld § 922(g)(3) as consistent with historical traditions of disarming dangerous persons, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of disarming those who pose a danger to themselves or others, and survives Second Amendment scrutiny even as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government cannot identify a sufficient historical tradition of disarming persons solely for drug use.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the Section 1 exemption for transportation workers, particularly whether last-mile delivery workers who distribute goods to retail stores are 'engaged in . . . interstate commerce.' This affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a wide range of distribution workers.

positions.label: Broad exemption — last-mile delivery workers qualify
positions.summary: Holds that workers who are part of a continuous interstate transportation chain, including those making last-mile deliveries of goods that have moved in interstate commerce, qualify as transportation workers exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow exemption — last-mile distributors do not qualify
positions.summary: Holds that distribution workers delivering goods locally to retail stores are not 'transportation workers engaged in . . . interstate commerce' under Section 1 because they are not themselves moving goods across state lines.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA creates a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits have held that RLUIPA, enacted under the Spending Clause, does not clearly authorize personal-liability damages against individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds, while others have allowed such claims to proceed.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA provides a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials sued in their individual capacities for violations of prisoners' religious exercise rights.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials because Congress cannot impose personal liability on non-recipient individuals through the Spending Clause.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
